contributions.statement: In GitHub Actions workflows that run an agent or LLM step (claude-code-action, codex-action, run-gemini-cli, ai-inference), do not let a step whose prompt contains issue, PR or comment text pass its free-form output (final-message, summary, response) to a later shell, gh or git step. Pass an identifier instead of the body, and validate the output against an allowlist or schema in a deterministic step before any write.
contributions.evidence: §VI-D Table VII: this agent-output-to-script path (P2S) appears in 419 of 496 author-confirmed exploitable workflows (84.5%), with direct prompt-to-agent paths in 103. 78.8% of cases end in GitHub write/API operations and 61.9% in shell/tool execution. Audit: 79.2% of cases involve actions/ai-inference and many effects are labels or comments; exploitability is judged by the authors without dynamic exploits.
relative_to: GitHub Security Lab guidance on untrusted input expansion in workflow scripts (pre-2026)
2608.06477 untrusted content treated as authorized instructions

contributions.statement: Before adopting a third-party AI GitHub Action, confirm it exposes caller-identity gating (allow-users, allowed_non_write_users or similar), set the gate to named maintainers or bots rather than '*', and add a workflow-level actor or author-association check, because most AI actions have no gate and workflow authors rarely add one.
contributions.evidence: §IV-C Table I-II: only 21 of 1,033 AI-assisted actions expose caller-identity controls, and 8 of the 10 most-used have none (properties LLM-inferred, 95.9% field agreement on 100 checked records). §VI-D/§VII-A: of 881 workflows with taint paths, 41.1% were blocked by some guard (34.7% action-level only) and only 6.4% had a workflow-level guard. Guards count as sanitizers by definition and were not attacked.
relative_to: least-privilege / restrict-who-can-trigger guidance for CI workflows (pre-2026)

contributions.statement: If you run CodeQL or a similar workflow taint checker on CI YAML, add rules that treat an AI step's outputs as tainted whenever its prompt is, because prompt-sink-only taint rules stop at the model boundary and cannot see the agent-output-to-script path.
contributions.evidence: §VI-B Table V: CodeQL and Argus given P2A sink specs covered 76 and 66 of 496 confirmed cases and 0 P2S. Table VI: disabling output bridging drops coverage from 496 to 103. Audit: coverage is computed only over TaintAWI's own confirmed set, and the baselines were barred from P2S by construction.

reason: Two moderate, directly transferable CI-hardening rules survive. They apply to any repo that wires agent steps into GitHub Actions, and their measured prevalence goes beyond the generic 'untrusted input' guidance. The detector-design practice rests on a self-referential comparison and stays weak. The paper says nothing about whether a workflow graph beats an open agent loop for coding work.
